name: Iris Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you tell me stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get to the benefits office on Mill Street at half seven, before the doors open, because that's the only quiet hour I get. I lead a team of six on disability benefit reviews, so I check their decisions, take the hardest cases myself and go on the home visits nobody else wants. The best bit is getting a wrongly cut claim put back. What wears me out is the backlog, about four hundred open reviews, and a phone that never stops.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you take the hardest cases yourself. What does a hard case look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Last month it was a man in his fifties with MS who'd been marked fit for work because he managed to walk into the assessment centre. Afterwards he sat in his car for twenty minutes, crying, because his legs had gone. None of that is on a form. You only find it out by sitting in someone's kitchen and asking the right questions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Tomas in a two-room flat above a launderette, and he drives a delivery van. Between us we cover the rent and not much else, and I've still got a big loan from my master's. I've maybe three weeks of money put by. Calder Falls lost the paper mill years ago, so there's nothing like my job within an hour's drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because the people we serve need a human, not a chatbot. At the union branch meeting I'd say the money that was meant for these systems should go into hiring, because we're two caseworkers short. Online I'd keep it fairly careful, because we're told not to post about the department.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, but it doesn't fix my life. I'm still on lower pay than people doing this job in the city, I've still got the loan, and the backlog still grows every winter. AI not working out just means the cuts come the old way, through hiring freezes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep pushing at the union for the two empty posts to be filled. I'd also try to put fifty a month aside, which sounds tiny but would be the first real saving I've ever had. I wouldn't touch any of the new software unless I was ordered to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with the same tiredness underneath. It's like hearing a storm went past the town, but your roof still leaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the cuts come the old way. Which cut worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hiring freeze. Our longest-serving caseworker, Bev, retires next spring, and I'm fairly sure her post just disappears. Then her ninety cases land on my team, and something gets missed, and it's always someone vulnerable who gets missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money stays this tight at home, what gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going out has already gone, really. Next would be the summer trip to see my mum at the coast, which is the one thing I'd hate to lose. Tomas and I have agreed we'd rather eat beans for a month than miss that.

say: The people we serve need **a human**, not a chatbot.
The money meant for AI systems should pay for **two missing caseworkers** instead.
think: I'm **relieved**, but low pay, the loan and the winter backlog all stay the same.
Without AI, the cuts still come through **hiring freezes**, just more quietly.
do: **Keep leading** the disability review team the way she does now.
Press the **union branch** to fill the two empty caseworker posts.
Save **fifty a month**, her first real saving, and avoid new software unless ordered.
S0.quote: AI not working out just means the cuts come the old way, through hiring freezes.
fieldNote: Even in the calm picture, she reads the future through **staffing cuts**, not technology.
Her thin cushion and **student loan** keep money worries alive whatever AI does.
She worries more for **vulnerable claimants** missed by an overloaded team than for herself.

steps.text: Keep running the disability review team and its home visits
Push the union branch to refill the two empty caseworker posts
Put fifty a month into savings for the first time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: a computer can't sit in someone's kitchen. At work I'd be the one asking, in every meeting, who checks the machine when it gets a decision wrong. Online I'd share the stories of people it gets wrong, without names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my team gets cut first, because writing decision letters and checking evidence is most of what we do on paper. They'd keep me longer as a lead, maybe, but as a supervisor of software, and I'd hate that. With a thin cushion and no other office nearby, I'd be one bad restructure away from real trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union to demand a written agreement before any system goes live: a human signs every refusal. I'd start paying down the smallest card and stop the gym, which is thirty a month. I suppose I'd have to go to the training they'd make us do, but I'd go dragging my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, mostly, and a bit sick. Angry because I know it'll be sold as saving money, and sick because I'd be watching good people on my team get letters like the ones we send out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth, who's forty-eight and the best letter writer I've ever met. Writing is exactly what this thing does, and she's got a sick husband at home. I'd fight for her harder than for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go to the training dragging your feet. If refusing hurt your job, would you still drag them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair, and it's the bit I don't like about myself. I'd probably learn just enough to keep my post and not one thing more. I'm not proud of that, but I'm not going to pretend I'd be keen.

say: A computer **can't sit** in a claimant's kitchen and see what's really wrong.
Someone must answer **who checks** the machine when it gets a decision wrong.
think: Her **team gets cut** first, because letters and evidence checks are most of its work.
With a **thin cushion** and no nearby office, one restructure could sink her.
do: Get the union to win a **written agreement** that a human signs every refusal.
Cancel the **thirty-a-month** gym and pay down the smallest card.
Attend the required **AI training**, learning only enough to keep her post.
feel: **Angry** that it will be sold as a saving.
**Sick** at picturing her own team getting cut letters.
S1.quote: My team gets cut first, because writing decision letters and checking evidence is most of what we do on paper.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that her job is **mostly thinking work**, and so is exposed early.
Her first instinct is **collective protection**, not personal escape.
She admits a **gap**: she'll resist the tools but learn the minimum if her post depends on it.

steps.text: Win a union agreement that a human signs every benefit refusal
Cancel the gym and pay off the smallest credit card
Sit the department's AI training and learn only the basics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice, not the weather. Somebody decides to replace a benefits office with a program, and that somebody should answer to voters. I'd be at every protest in the square outside the town hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished in this job within two years. Everything I do at a desk, the reading, weighing evidence, writing the decision, is exactly what they say it can do. The home visits are the only hands-on bit, and even that's three years from a robot, which isn't long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop paying anything extra on the loan and keep every pound I could. I'd go full time on the union side, organising the office before the cuts land, because two years isn't long enough to retrain into anything. Tomas and I would talk about moving in with my mum at the coast if the rent got beyond us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, properly. I'm twenty-seven and I'd be watching the only career I trained for vanish before I've even paid for the degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you did move in with your mum, what would that mean for you and Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be hard on us. My mum's place is tiny and Tomas would have to find driving work there, which is pretty much the only thing that might last a bit longer. I'd hate going backwards like that, but I'd rather be cramped than homeless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the claimants you've helped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to tell them to get every claim in now, while a person still reads it. I couldn't say that out loud at work, but I'd think it every single day.

say: Replacing a benefits office is **a choice**, and someone should answer to voters.
She'd join **every protest** in the square outside the town hall.
think: She expects to be **finished** in the job within **two years**.
Home visits are her only hands-on work, and **robots** follow just three years later.
do: Stop **extra loan payments** and hold on to every pound.
Organise the office through the **union** before the cuts land.
Plan with Tomas to **move in** with her mum at the coast if needed.
feel: **Frightened**, watching her career vanish before her **degree** is paid off.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven and I'd be watching the only career I trained for vanish before I've even paid for the degree.
fieldNote: The **two-year warning** leaves her no time to retrain, so she turns to organising.
Her escape plan relies on **family**, not savings, because she has almost none.
She knows her job is **desk work** first, with home visits only buying a little time.

steps.text: Stop extra student loan payments and keep every pound as cash
Organise the benefits office through the union before the cuts
Join the protests outside the town hall
Move in with her mum at the coast if rent becomes impossible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but louder, because five years means there's time to do something. I'd tell the branch we have five years to write the rules, not two. I'd post about it more, because people would actually be paying attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to see it coming and not quite enough to dodge it. I'd probably still lose this job, but maybe I could move into something where the person in the room matters, like advocacy for disabled people. Even that's thinking work, so I'm not sure it's safe, and I hate guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first couple of years I'd look at the charity advocacy posts, though there are only two in the whole county. I'd save harder, maybe sixty a month, and sell the old car and use Tomas's van. I'd also put my name forward for the union's national committee on technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still scared, but less trapped. Five years is a window, even if it's a small one with a draught coming through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even advocacy is thinking work. So what's the plan if that goes too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't have one, honestly. I keep coming back to care work, because that's people in rooms, but the pay is even worse than mine. I'd be choosing between a job a computer can do and a job I can't afford to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools at all now. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose it'd be silly not to know what I'm up against. I'd probably read about it rather than use it. I just don't want to train the thing that replaces Ruth and me.

say: Five years gives **time to write** the rules, so the union must act now.
People would finally be **paying attention**, so she'd post more about it.
think: Five years lets her **see it coming** but probably not dodge it.
Even **advocacy work** is thinking work, so nothing feels safe.
do: Apply for one of the county's **two advocacy posts** at a charity.
Save **sixty a month** and sell her old car.
Stand for the union's **national committee** on technology.
feel: **Scared**, but less trapped than with two years.
S3.quote: I'd be choosing between a job a computer can do and a job I can't afford to do.
fieldNote: Extra time **widens her options** but doesn't change where she thinks it ends.
Her resistance to AI tools is partly **loyalty** to colleagues like Ruth.
Care work appeals to her values but **pay** makes it feel impossible.

steps.text: Apply for the disability advocacy posts at the county charity
Sell the old car and save sixty a month
Stand for the union's national committee on technology

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so there's no excuse for doing it badly. In the branch I'd push for retraining money written into the deal. Online I'd talk about guaranteed income, because I've seen what happens when people fall through the cracks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels almost survivable. At thirty-seven I'd be old enough to know things and young enough to start again, but I've no savings to start again with. So I'd need the government or the union to pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the job for now and build up the loan payments again, since the debt would be gone sooner. Over the first year I'd look into a part-time course in occupational therapy, because that's hands-on and close to what I do. I'd keep refusing to use AI at work until there's an agreement about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than scared. A decade is long enough that I can make a plan, but I'm already worn out by the job I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why occupational therapy, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the best moments in my job are in people's homes, working out how they can get up the stairs or back to work. An occupational therapist does that with their hands, and robots come three years after the thinking AI. I'm not daft enough to think it's forever, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for a course on your salary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I couldn't, not without help. I'd go to the evening classes at the college in Ashby and hope the union's retraining fund covers the fees. If it didn't, I'd probably just keep putting it off, which is what I do with most things that scare me.

say: Ten years leaves **no excuse** for handling it badly.
Any deal must include **retraining money**, and the country should look at **guaranteed income**.
think: At **thirty-seven** she could start again, but she has **no savings** to do it.
She'd need the **government or union** to fund a career change.
do: Stay in the job and **pay down** the student loan faster.
Look into a part-time **occupational therapy** course at the Ashby college.
Refuse AI tools at work until there's a **union agreement**.
feel: **Tired** more than scared, already worn down by the current job.
S4.quote: At thirty-seven I'd be old enough to know things and young enough to start again, but I've no savings to start again with.
fieldNote: With a decade, she picks a **hands-on career** that robots reach later.
Her plan rests on **outside funding**, and she admits she may keep putting it off.
Fatigue with her **current workload** colours every scenario.

steps.text: Keep her caseworker job while the change is still years away
Raise student loan payments to clear the debt sooner
Enrol in an evening occupational therapy course at the Ashby college
Push for retraining money in the union's agreement with the department

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without any doubt. Two years isn't time to retrain, save or even argue properly, and I've got three weeks of money. What would help is a guarantee from the department that nobody is let go without a paid year of retraining, and a public body that checks every automated benefit decision.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the claimants, and they're who I really worry about. If the machines get my job, fine, I'll survive somehow. If the machines get benefit decisions wrong, a disabled man like the one I visited ends up with nothing, and nobody's in the kitchen to notice.

headlineQuote: If the machines get benefit decisions wrong, a disabled man like the one I visited ends up with nothing, and nobody's in the kitchen to notice.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old team lead** on disability benefit reviews in Calder Falls, a former paper-mill town.
She lives with her partner Tomas, carries a **master's loan** and has about **three weeks** of savings.
A committed **union member**, she answers every scenario by organising colleagues and demanding human checks.
She refuses AI tools and sees her **desk-based job** as exposed early, with home visits buying little time.
Her fear grows sharply with **less warning**, and she leans on family and union funding for any escape.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time to retrain or save on almost no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed **paid year** of retraining for anyone let go.
A public body that **checks every** automated benefit decision.
